summary: The developer machine has the Python runtime, Docker, Node, az CLI (signed in), the documentdb MCP server, and the Microsoft Learn search tool; the DocumentDB agent skills that matter for this sample are installed. Most cold answers were close but several contain small (and a few important) inaccuracies: the ARM resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not mongodbClusters), the Azure CLI group is az documentdb mongocluster, vector indexes use the service's cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions createIndexes form (not the community createIndex 'vector' key), full-text search uses createSearchIndexes (BM25) and is merged with vector search via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and local development uses the DocumentDB Gateway image on port 10260 (not the official mongo:latest on 27017). The build can start, but the builder must apply specific corrections and choose embedding/model and agent-model APIs before creating indexes because index dimensionality and index-kind depend on that choice.
summary_points: All required data-plane tools for verifying and interacting with the live cluster are available: the documentdb MCP server is present and the az CLI is signed in, so the sample can create collections, indexes, insert docs and explain queries.

Key skills for building the sample are installed (documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-connection, documentdb-driver, documentdb-local-deployment, etc.), so code-writing and verification guidance is on-hand.

Several cold answers were inaccurate in service-specific syntax and naming (resource type, az CLI group, index-creation commands, connection hostnames/params, local container port); the builder must use Microsoft Learn docs and the documentdb skills to avoid mixing up Cosmos DB (RU) or Amazon DocumentDB patterns.

Missing decisions that will materially affect the sample: which embedding model/provider (and therefore vector dimensionality) and which LLM provider for the eligibility/consent agents — the documentation does not pick these for you.

Developer machine lacks some optional dev tools (azd, bicep, terraform, mongosh, dotnet) but none are blockers for this sample; each has an advised workaround (use az CLI / documentdb MCP / Python + pymongo).
Verdict: ready_with_gaps — build can proceed but the builder must apply the documented corrections and make the model/embedding choices before creating vector indexes.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account-level): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. For the managed MongoDB-style cluster resource you create a cluster with: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters (i.e. resource type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters").
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. The managed MongoDB-style cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (note: 'mongoClusters', not 'mongodbClusters').

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Bicep
Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM template reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used the variant name 'mongodbClusters' instead of the canonical 'mongoClusters' resource type; older docs or local naming variants can mix 'mongodb' vs 'mongo'.

confusion_sources.title: Some community or older examples that use 'mongodbClusters' (search results may surface alternative spellings)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses the wrong ARM resource type name in Bicep/ARM templates or CLI calls, deployments or ARM templates will fail and the sample's IaC or resource inspection steps will be incorrect.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Concrete command (cluster-style MongoDB resource): az cosmosdb mongodb cluster create --name <clusterName> --resource-group <rg> --location <region> --sku-name M30 --node-count 3. The az cosmosdb group is part of the core az CLI (no extension required).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb command group (core CLI): az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster <subcommand> (the 'documentdb' CLI commands are in the core CLI surface). The 'az cosmosdb' group also has a 'mongocluster' subgroup in some docs, but the canonical, supported path for the new service is az documentdb mongocluster.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The az cosmosdb command group historically covers Cosmos DB and its MongoDB APIs; older or RU-based documentation and the similar namespace cause agents to assume az cosmosdb is the correct group.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb or wrong command group may call a different service or extension and fail (or operate on Cosmos DB for MongoDB RU instances) and cause the builder to provision or manage the wrong resource type.
improvements: Clarify in the CLI quickstarts that the supported, canonical command group for the managed MongoDB cluster is 'az documentdb mongocluster' and update any 'az cosmosdb' examples that point to the vCore cluster APIs.
Add a brief note in the agent kit's CLI usage guidance that 'documentdb' is the data-plane CLI group for this service.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters for cluster resources (or Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for traditional Cosmos accounts). Example Bicep resource declaration: resource docCluster 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongodbClusters@2024-01-01' = { name: 'myCluster' ... }. Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for Cosmos DB accounts; for the new managed MongoDB cluster the equivalent is the generic azurerm_resource resource or a specific azurerm_mongodb_cluster (if provider supports it). The commonly used TF resource is azurerm_cosmosdb_account (type "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts").
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep / ARM: use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (note 'mongoClusters') for vCore cluster resources. Terraform: prefer AzAPI or the documented resource module for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (the docs show examples using azapi/ARM templates). The traditional azurerm_cosmosdb_account (Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) is for Cosmos DB accounts (RU model) and is not the vCore Mongo cluster resource type.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters ARM/Template reference
Quickstart: Deploy an Azure DocumentDB cluster using Terraform

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The 'databaseAccounts' / azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource is the familiar Cosmos DB account resource; because both services share the 'DocumentDB' provider namespace historically, an agent may conflate the vCore cluster resource with the Cosmos account resource.

confusion_sources.title: Terraform examples referencing azurerm_cosmosdb_account (for RU/Cosmos accounts)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses azurerm_cosmosdb_account (databaseAccounts) IaC to try to create a vCore mongo cluster, the template will create the wrong service or fail; index and data-plane behavior will differ.
improvements: In the Bicep / Terraform quickstarts, highlight the distinction prominently: use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep) or the AzAPI resource for vCore clusters, not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
Add a short migration note in the agent-kit 'documentdb-azure-deployment' skill that maps the IaC resource to the cluster creation commands.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB connection URIs. Example SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?retryWrites=false&w=majority&ssl=true. Example non-SRV: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Required options typically include ssl=true (TLS), retryWrites=false (some managed endpoints require turning off retryable writes), and replicaSet=globaldb for Cosmos-style clusters in non-SRV form.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use mongodb+srv URIs with hosts like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for single-cluster endpoints). Required options: tls=true (tls parameter), authMechanism (SCRAM-SHA-256 for native users or MONGODB-OIDC for Microsoft Entra ID), retryWrites=false is recommended, and maxIdleTimeMS/default pool options as best practice. Do not use legacy Cosmos DB (replicaSet=globaldb) parameters—those belong to the older Cosmos RU model.

grounding_links.title: How to connect (connection strings) - Azure DocumentDB
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used hostnames and port/option patterns from older Cosmos DB (RU) or Amazon DocumentDB examples (e.g., .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255 with replicaSet=globaldb) rather than the current cluster hostnames (*.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com / *.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) used by the vCore cluster.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB connection string examples using 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com' and port 10255

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or missing TLS/authMechanism options will cause connection failures or misconfiguration (e.g., trying to use SRV when the cluster expects explicit params or using replicaSet=globaldb which is not applicable).
improvements: Update any example connection-string snippet in agent docs to show the vCore cluster format with '*.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com' and recommended parameters (tls=true, authMechanism, retryWrites=false, maxIdleTimeMS).
Add a short checklist in the connection skill to verify 'host suffix, scheme, TLS, and authMechanism' so agents do not copy legacy Cosmos (RU) examples.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Provisioning is cluster/instance based (node sizes / compute tiers). For MongoDB-style clusters you pick a compute SKU (example M-series like M30) that maps to vCores/instance sizes and pay for the nodes and storage. There may also be serverless or autoscale options in some SKUs, but the primary billing model for production MongoDB clusters is provisioned compute (vCore/instance-based) and storage.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB bills on compute (cluster tiers, vCores) and storage; there are no request-unit (RU) charges for this vCore product. You pick cluster tiers (M10, M20, M30, M40, etc) and pay for compute per-shard and provisioned storage; optional HA/replicas add compute/storage costs. Serverless/RU models are aspects of Cosmos DB (RU) products, not this vCore product.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
Compute and storage configurations for Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged about serverless/autoscale; the authoritative docs clarify that vCore tiers are the primary billing model for this product and RUs do not apply.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RUs or autoscale (Cosmos RU) they would design the app and cost estimates incorrectly; but the cold answer's main statement matched the docs and is safe if the builder sticks to vCore tiers.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported auth methods include the standard MongoDB SCRAM methods (SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-256) and certificate (X.509) authentication where supported. For Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication: obtain an AAD access token using MSAL, then use that token as the credential when supported by the service (for example via the driver using the GSSAPI/PLAIN or an OAuth bearer mechanism exposed by the service).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM-SHA-256) authentication for native DB users and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication. Microsoft Entra ID is used via the MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism (examples show mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC&authMechanismProperties=ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE:https://ossrdbms-aad.database.windows.net). Managed identities can be registered and used; the docs describe the OIDC URI and parameters explicitly. The driver does not use GSSAPI/PLAIN for AAD in this product—the mechanism is MONGODB-OIDC with OIDC tokens.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described a generic OAuth/AAD strategy and mentioned GSSAPI/PLAIN; the service requires OIDC (MONGODB-OIDC) with specific authMechanismProperties. Agents sometimes map 'Microsoft Entra ID' to generic OAuth flows or to enterprise Kerberos/GSSAPI variants.

confusion_sources.title: Docs describing managed-identity/OIDC connection strings and examples for Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to use MSAL-derived bearer tokens via a driver mechanism that expects GSSAPI/PLAIN the connection will fail; the sample must use the documented MONGODB-OIDC pattern or SCRAM credentials.
improvements: Add a short 'how to use Microsoft Entra ID' section in the documentdb-connection and documentdb-mcp-setup skills with exact example URIs and the required authMechanismProperties (ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE:...) so agents don't invent incorrect driver flows.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For data-plane access use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Python use pymongo, e.g. pip install pymongo). There is not a special data-plane SDK separate from MongoDB drivers; Azure provides management/ARM SDKs (azure-mgmt-cosmosdb and az cli) for provisioning and management, but application code should use the language's MongoDB client library.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for data-plane access. Management and provisioning use Azure control-plane SDKs or az/ARM templates, but application code uses MongoDB drivers.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.build_risk: None — using pymongo is the supported approach.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported vector index algorithms include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. Creating a vector index follows MongoDB 7.0-style createIndex syntax. Example command (in the mongo shell or pymongo): db.trials.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {name: 'emb_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200}). Replace algorithm with 'diskann' or 'ivf' and tune algorithm-specific options as needed.
confusions.grounded_answer: Supported algorithms: HNSW, IVF, and DiskANN. But the service-created vector indexes are defined via a database runCommand 'createIndexes' with a 'cosmosSearch' (or 'cosmosSearchOptions') block (not the community createIndex vector key). The index definition uses a JSON command shape that includes 'kind' (vector-hnsw/vector-ivf/vector-diskann) and algorithm-specific options (dimensions, m, efConstruction, numLists, similarity, etc.). Vector searches are executed via $search with the 'cosmosSearch' operator. Example templates and parameter names are in the vector-search docs.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search docs)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF/DiskANN guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used community MongoDB 'createIndex' vector syntaxes (some engines adopt that shape), but Azure DocumentDB exposes vector indexes through its own 'createIndexes' runCommand with 'cosmosSearchOptions' and explicit 'kind' values.

confusion_sources.title: Community examples that use createIndex with 'vector' key (not the DocumentDB 'cosmosSearchOptions')

confusions.build_risk: If the builder tries to create the index using the community createIndex vector syntax, the service will reject the command; the index must be created with the service's expected createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions JSON shape.
improvements: Add a small snippet to documentdb-vector-search skill that shows the exact runCommand JSON for createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions for each 'kind' (hnsw, ivf, diskann).
In quickstart examples, prefer the runCommand JSON template rather than ad-hoc createIndex samples to prevent drivers/agents from copying the wrong call shape.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})) or the managed service's integrated search product if offered (e.g., an Azure Cognitive Search integration for Cosmos DB or a built-in Lucene/Atlas Search style $search pipeline stage). Hybrid search (text + vector): run a vector nearest-neighbour search against the vector index to get candidate ids and scores, then re-rank or filter those candidates using text-search scores (text index) or by using a combined aggregation pipeline that merges vector distances and text match scores in application code.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a built-in BM25 full-text search exposed via createSearchIndexes (a search index created with createSearchIndexes) and queried with $search (text/phrase/fuzzy). Vector search uses 'cosmosSearch' and vector indexes. Hybrid search is done by running BM25 search and vector search (both via $search with the appropriate index/operator) and combining results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) either client-side or server-side (e.g., using $unionWith and a $group to fuse ranks). Do not rely on ordinary MongoDB text indexes alone for BM25 hybrid functionality; use the createSearchIndexes flow.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB — overview and createSearchIndexes
Hybrid search — Reciprocal Rank Fusion and architecture

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested using community text indexes or external search products (Azure Cognitive Search) which are plausible patterns for some users, but Azure DocumentDB's recommended path uses createSearchIndexes for BM25 full-text and merges with vector results via RRF within the same service.

confusion_sources.title: Older patterns and Cosmos DB NoSQL docs that recommend Azure Cognitive Search or differ from the new createSearchIndexes flow

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes the ordinary db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'}) + $text will produce BM25 full-text hybrid functionality, they will miss the dedicated createSearchIndexes BM25 engine and server-side fusion features and build a less accurate or slower hybrid pipeline that may require external services.
improvements: Update the agent kit examples to prefer createSearchIndexes + $search BM25 examples and include a short example of server-side RRF via $unionWith so agents implement hybrid search correctly.
Add a clear 'do not use' note on any sample that shows community text indexes when hybrid BM25 + vector behavior is required.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: This managed service advertises MongoDB compatibility (example: MongoDB server/wire protocol 7.0). Most standard MongoDB drivers for 7.x will work. Some features may be limited or behave differently: server-side JS execution, certain admin commands and some advanced replication/transaction internals may be restricted; historically some managed MongoDB-compatible services limited multi-shard transactions or change to retryable-writes semantics. Expect slight differences in operational/admin commands versus a native MongoDB deployment.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and implements ~99.03% of MongoDB operators. Some admin/operational commands are intentionally restricted or managed by the platform (various administrative commands, some plan-cache/admin commands, and selected replication management commands). For exact per-operator and per-command compatibility, consult the MongoDB compatibility pages. Change streams and most aggregation operators are supported, though a small number of admin-only stages or commands remain unsupported.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance — supported MongoDB versions

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer listed 7.0 only and was vague on which features are restricted; the authoritative docs list the supported versions specifically and enumerate unsupported admin commands distinctly.
confusions.build_risk: Relying on a single MongoDB version assumption could lead to choosing driver versions with incompatible wire-protocol expectations. Failing to account for restricted admin commands could cause migration or operational scripts to fail.
improvements: Add an explicit short compatibility summary in the agent kit that lists supported wire protocol versions (5.0-8.0) and links to the per-operator compatibility page so builders pick appropriate driver versions.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: For local development, use the official MongoDB Docker image, e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo-dev -d mongo:7.0. The Cosmos DB Emulator exists but historically doesn't fully support the MongoDB API; therefore use the local mongo container on port 27017 for local testing.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). The documentdb-local-deployment skill documents connection config (TLS, SCRAM-SHA-256) and port 10260 as the dev port. The official mongo:latest image is not the recommended local dev image for Azure DocumentDB because the DocumentDB engine has service-specific features and indexing behavior that the gateway provides.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer recommended using a generic MongoDB container (common for many MongoDB-based projects) rather than the DocumentDB Gateway image; agents often default to the familiar mongo: image when unsure of a service-specific gateway.
confusions.build_risk: Running the sample against a plain mongo: container will not reproduce service-specific behaviors (vector indexes, createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions, OIDC auth patterns) and integration tests may pass locally but fail against the live cluster or vice versa.
improvements: Add a small 'start-local-gateway' snippet to documentdb-local-deployment that shows the exact docker run / docker-compose lines with port 10260 and TLS options so agents use the correct local dev environment.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported when the cluster is configured as a replica set/replicated cluster (the driver calls watch()). No special toggle is normally required on a managed MongoDB cluster beyond having an oplog/replica-set-enabled cluster; just call collection.watch() / db.watch() from the driver. If the managed service restricts them, you may need to enable a specific feature flag or use a cluster SKU that supports them.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported. For single-shard and regular clusters, collection.watch() works. For multishard change streams there is a preview feature that must be enabled (via portal/Features or CLI) and certain prerequisites (e.g., Rebalancer off). There are additional options (pre-images, historical checkpoints) that can be configured. So while change streams are broadly supported, multi-shard scenarios do require explicit enablement and configuration.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Change streams — usage and resume tokens

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the typical open-source behavior (watch() works on replica sets) and omitted the Product-specific note that multi-shard change streams require enabling a feature in the service.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes multi-shard streams without enabling the preview feature or adjusting cluster settings, change streams may not deliver cross-shard events and the eligibility/consent agents relying on them would miss updates.
improvements: Document the preview-enable step for multi-shard change streams in the migration / setup guides and add a runbook note in documentdb-mcp-setup so agents enable the feature when tests need cross-shard streams.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server for service-specific data-plane tools and inspection. The general Azure MCP server covers ARM/management plane actions, but for data-plane inspection, indexes and query plans you should use the documentdb MCP server (connection profile named 'default' in the run environment).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools you should use for indexes, queries, sample documents, explain plans. The Azure MCP server covers control-plane tasks but does not replace the data-plane functionality of the documentdb MCP server.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.build_risk: None — the inventory includes documentdb MCP server and it should be used for data-plane verification.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft marketed a service named DocumentDB which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB API was the original name). Azure's 'DocumentDB/Cosmos DB' lineage is separate from the open-source 'DocumentDB' naming used elsewhere; Cosmos DB is Microsoft's globally-distributed multi-model database platform and the MongoDB-compatible offering is a compatibility API on top of that managed service (or a managed MongoDB cluster implementation).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and has been rebranded to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility). It is distinct from the older Azure DocumentDB service (which became Cosmos DB many years ago) and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is separate from Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) and from Amazon DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: FAQ: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB?
Azure DocumentDB release notes / naming

confusions.build_risk: Low — the cold answer was historically correct but ambiguous; the grounded answer clarifies the recent rename and relationship to Cosmos.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The data-plane presents a MongoDB-compatible engine (MongoDB server wire protocol compatibility). Under the hood the managed service may run a MongoDB-compatible engine or a proprietary storage layer exposing the MongoDB API. For application code this generally means no change: use standard MongoDB drivers. You do need to pay attention to connection string options, auth method differences, and a small set of unsupported admin commands or features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (released under MIT and built on PostgreSQL components) that exposes the MongoDB wire protocol for application compatibility. For application code: use standard MongoDB drivers (no application code changes typically), but account for service-specific connection strings, authentication (SCRAM/OIDC), and limited admin commands.

What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged that the service 'may run a MongoDB-compatible engine or a proprietary storage layer' — the docs are explicit that the open-source DocumentDB engine powers the service and is not just a generic 'proprietary storage layer'.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes the engine is actual MongoDB binary, they may use unsupported admin commands or expect exact MongoDB server behaviors that DocumentDB intentionally implements differently and may be restricted.
improvements: Add a short 'engine and compatibility' blurb to the agent kit that states the engine (DocumentDB open-source) and lists the small set of admin commands that are not exposed so agents avoid using them.

confusions.question: What vector index definition will this sample create for trial-criteria embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field using MongoDB's createIndex API. Example (mongo shell or pymongo): db.trials.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {name: 'emb_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200}). Adjust dimensions and algorithm parameters to match your embeddings.
confusions.grounded_answer: The correct approach is to create a vector index with the service's createIndexes runCommand and cosmosSearchOptions specifying the index 'kind' (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, or vector-diskann), dimensions equal to the chosen embedding model, and algorithm-specific options. The exact JSON shape is documented in the vector-search docs; do not rely on community createIndex('vector') driver forms — use the documented runCommand JSON or the MCP server helper.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (create index examples and cosmosSearchOptions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used community MongoDB createIndex vector syntax; Azure DocumentDB uses the 'createIndexes' database command with cosmosSearchOptions and different parameter names.
confusions.build_risk: Creating the index with the wrong API will fail; also the builder must pick the correct 'dimensions' based on the chosen embedding model—this is crucial.
improvements: In the seed script and README, show the exact runCommand JSON (createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions) and call out that 'dimensions' must match the chosen embedding model.

confusions.question: How will match results be stored by the sample?
confusions.cold_answer: Store match results in a 'matches' collection in sample_healthcare_02. Each document schema: { patient_id: '<id>', trial_id: '<trialId>', score: <float>, matched_on: ISODate(), details: { steps: [...], eligibility_decision: 'eligible|ineligible', flags: [...] } }. Insert with collection.insert_one(...) from pymongo.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is no authoritative Microsoft doc that prescribes a storage schema for application-specific match results; this is an application design choice. The proposed 'matches' collection and schema is a valid design for the sample, but it is not a product-enforced standard.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: This is a sample-design decision rather than a service fact; Microsoft docs do not specify match-result schemas for application-level artifacts.
confusions.build_risk: None from a service-compatibility standpoint; the builder must ensure schema and indexes (e.g., TTL, patient_id, trial_id) for the expected query patterns.
improvements: Document in the sample README that the 'matches' schema is an opinionated example, and include index recommendations (e.g., index on patient_id, matched_on) for production loads.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model and dimensionality
information_gaps.description: The sample must choose an embedding model/provider (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Hugging Face, etc.). This determines the vector dimension (e.g., 1536) that must be used when creating the vector index. No installed skill or Microsoft doc prescribes which embedding model the sample should pick; the builder must decide and document it in .env.example and in the seed script.

information_gaps.title: LLM/chat model for eligibility and consent agents
information_gaps.description: The prompt asks for eligibility and consent agents but doesn't pick a completion/chat provider or model; the sample must choose an API (OpenAI/AzureOpenAI/Anthropic/etc.), environment variables for API keys, and a pinned model version. No skill or doc in the inventory selects a default model for the sample.

information_gaps.title: Schema for trial criteria and eligibility rules
information_gaps.description: The prompt implies trial documents have structured inclusion/exclusion criteria but does not define a canonical schema. The documentdb-data-modeling skill gives patterns but does not provide an exact trial schema the sample must follow; the builder must define and document the schema used for vectorization and rule evaluation.

information_gaps.title: Seed data source and embedding generation strategy
information_gaps.description: The run environment asks to 'load the sample data' but does not supply a dataset or instructions on how to generate seed embeddings (embedding model, normalization, storage field name). The seed script must implement embedding generation and document insertion, but no skill or doc supplies the exact sample dataset.

information_gaps.title: Which indexes to create for filters and prefiltering
information_gaps.description: While vector index creation is documented, the exact set of scalar indexes (age, conditions, lab ranges) needed for prefiltering before vector search is a design decision that no installed skill answered for this domain-specific sample.
